title: Mark Mortimer, ‘Another World’ Soap Opera Star, Dies at 59
description:

body:
Mark Mortimer, best known for his role as Nick Hudson on the soap opera “Another World,” died Sept. 23 after a battle with cancer. He was 59.

	“Mark Mortimer lived many lives in one lifetime,” his family wrote in his online obituary. “He was an Army veteran, a model, an actor, an entrepreneur and a builder. He was a husband, father, son, brother and friend. He was curious and determined, willing to take chances, start something new, change direction and figure things out along the way. But of all the titles Mark held throughout his life, the two that mattered most to him were husband and dad.”
	

	Born on April 15, 1967, in Yorkville, Ill., Mortimer began his acting career in 1996 with his role as Nick in “Another World,” in which he appeared in 81 episodes over three years. He also guest starred on “Spin City” in 1999 and acted in films like “The Nowhere Man” in 2005 before finishing his on-screen career.


	Mortimer was diagnosed with cancer in 2024. That same year, he and his wife, Christie, created the Integrative Access Foundation to give people facing cancer access to integrative therapies that might otherwise be financially out of reach. In addition to his acting career, Mortimer served in the United States Army, modeled and created the company Inside Out Construction.

	He is survived by Christie, his daughter Hunter, his mother Sharlene Pearson, father Emil Mortimer and siblings Michael Mortimer, Michele Doyle, Martin Mortimer, Melissa Gassmann, David Mortimer and Tyler Mortimer.

	“Mark loved being Hunter’s dad,” Mortimer’s family wrote in the obituary. “He was honest with her. He was present. And everything he did as her father was filled with love. When Hunter was little, Mark put her to bed every night. As she grew, he made the deliberate choice to build his life around being her father. He didn’t fit fatherhood in; he scheduled his work life around fatherhood. Being there for Hunter was never something Mark squeezed into his schedule. She was the schedule.”

schema.headline: Mark Mortimer, ‘Another World’ Soap Opera Star, Dies at 59

title: Slayyyter to Release ‘Brother Album’ to ‘Wor$t Girl in America’: ‘Wor$t Man in America’
description: Slayyyter has announced that “Wor$t Man in America,” the “brother” album to “Wor$t Girl in America,” is slated for release on December 4 via RECORDS
body:
Slayyyter has announced that “Wor$t Man in America,” the “brother” album to “Wor$t Girl in America,” is slated for release on December 4 via RECORDS/Columbia Records.

	“Wor$t Man in America” is being touted not as a new album, but rather a “brother” album to her third record “Wor$t Girl in America,” which was released on March 27. A press release describes it as a “counterpart to its predecessor” and “introduces contrasting visuals and a fresh perspective on the themes and ideas explored in the project before it.”
	

	“Some songs act as direct inversions, while others revisit familiar ideas from an entirely new angle, creating a parallel narrative that both mirrors and challenges the original project,” reads the release.


	Slayyyter has been teasing “Wor$t Man in America” since she launched her tour in July. During opening night in Missouri, she debuted the project’s first single “brand new chanel$” as well as additional cuts “nekromantik!,” “crank 2” and “i think he’s got a girl,” all of which are included on “Wor$t Man in America.” She followed later that week with the official release of “brand new chanel$,” and in September, she dropped the official version of “crank 2” on streaming.

	Slayyyter’s announcement comes just a day after she closed out the U.S. leg of her “Worst Girl in the World” tour in Brooklyn. The pop singer is on a red-hot run as part of her breakout year that continues with sold-out dates in Europe and the United Kingdom.

title: CAA Names Dasha Smith as Chief Operating Officer, Joins Agency From NFL
description:
CAA has named Dasha Smith as the new chief operating officer, following her tenure at the National Football League. 

	At the NFL, Smith was executi
body:
CAA has named Dasha Smith as the new chief operating officer, following her tenure at the National Football League. 

	At the NFL, Smith was executive VP, chief administrative officer, working as a member of commissioner Roger Goodell’s executive operating committee. During her tenure, Smith helped shape the league’s enterprise strategy and oversaw a broad portfolio of business functions, including technology, AI and innovation, data and analytics, strategy and business intelligence, human resources, inclusion, social responsibility and philanthropy and league office administration.
	

	“Dasha is a remarkably talented, accomplished and energetic leader with a deep understanding of how global organizations operate at their very best,” said CAA co-chairman and CEO Bryan Lourd. “We look forward to welcoming her to our senior management team and benefiting from her significant experience helping to guide leading media and sports organizations.”


	Added Smith: “I have tremendous respect for the industry leadership position that CAA and its management team continue to build on every year. Even greater is my appreciation for its widely admired, consistent mission to deliver the best possible service and resources to its clients. Joining a culture with that kind of clarity and purpose is an extraordinary opportunity.”

	Prior to the NFL, Smith was executive VP, global chief human resources officer for Sony Music Entertainment, and managing director, office of the chairman, at the global investment firm GCM Grosvenor. Smith also spent 10 years at WarnerMedia’s Time Inc., where she led global employee relations and employment law functions. She also served as a senior attorney in Time, Inc.’s business and legal affairs department, focusing on M&A. Smith began her legal career at Latham & Watkins, Covington & Burling, and Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison.

schema.headline: CAA Names Dasha Smith as Chief Operating Officer, Joins Agency From NFL

title: Hollywood Unions Warn of 25-Year Decline in U.S. Production Market Share
description: A coalition of Hollywood unions issued a report on Monday warning that the U.S. has lost significant market share in film and TV production over the
body:
A coalition of Hollywood unions issued a report on Monday warning that the U.S. has lost significant market share in film and TV production over the last 25 years.

	The report found that studios spent 74% of their film production budgets in the U.S. 25 years ago, but that the figure has since declined to 42%. On the TV side, the figure has fallen from 94% to 64%.

	The unions — including IATSE, the Directors Guild of America and SAG-AFTRA — published the report as Congress is considering whether to offer a 20%-30% production incentive to revive the domestic film and TV industry. Supporters have argued that the U.S. needs to counter generous incentives offered by Canada, the U.K., and other countries, and that state-based subsidies are inadequate.
	

	Members of Congress have focused on the sharp downturn in domestic production jobs since the end of Peak TV in 2022. But the union report, prepared by EY, takes a longer-term view, showing that the globalization of production has been underway since the turn of the millennium.


	The report acknowledges that production has grown considerably over that period — so the U.S. is taking a smaller piece of a much larger pie.

	The study looks only at films with budgets of $5 million or more, in 2025 dollars, and TV episodes costing at least $1 million, for those 40 minutes or shorter, and at least $1.7 million for episodes longer than 40 minutes. 

	In film, the report found that overall production spending by major studios rose from $3 billion to $7 billion annually in the last 25 years. And in TV, spending exploded from $933 million to $8.4 billion over the same span. The report acknowledges that the TV landscape has changed so dramatically over the past two decades that it is hard to draw clear comparisons.
	

	“The rise of streaming fundamentally altered production scale, budgets, season lengths, and release models, creating discontinuities in what constitutes a comparable television series across periods,” the authors wrote.

	The report is also limited in that it does not attempt to explain why production has shifted overseas — only to quantify the shift.

	The report finds that big-budget films account for much of the exodus. For the 25 most expensive films, the U.S. market share declined from 74% to 34% over the 25-year span. Those 25 films represented a quarter of all films produced by the major studios, but half of the crew and two-thirds of the budgets.

	“This highlights that production budgets are heavily concentrated within a small subset of films,” the report notes. “Patterns observed within this group generally reflect the broader analysis trends, albeit with a somewhat larger decline.”

	The report argues that if U.S. market share had held constant over the last 25 years, an additional $4 billion would be spent each year on TV and film production in the U.S.

	The Motion Picture Association issued its own report last month, arguing that a federal incentive would generate an additional $22 billion in annual domestic production spending by 2035. The MPA report did not attempt to measure the historical trend in market share, but did warn that market share will decline in the future if Congress does not act.

	The unions are set to hold a rally with Sen. Adam Schiff and many Democratic members of the California Congressional delegation on Tuesday in Glendale. Schiff and others last month introduced a federal credit that would combine with state-based subsidies to create the world’s most generous incentive regime.

	With support from President Trump, who came out in favor of the idea in August, backers are hoping to pass the incentive into law by the end of the year.

schema.headline: Hollywood Unions Warn of 25-Year Decline in U.S. Production Market Share

title: David Zaslav Bids Farewell to Warner Bros. Employees in Video on Eve of Skydance Merger Close: ‘It’s Been a Great Honor to Be Alongside All of You’
description: David Zaslav, four and a half years after closing the debt-burdened deal that formed Warner Bros. Discovery, is bidding farewell to the company’s em
body:
David Zaslav, four and a half years after closing the debt-burdened deal that formed Warner Bros. Discovery, is bidding farewell to the company’s employees as it is about to get swallowed up by David Ellison’s Paramount — to create a media giant saddled with even more debt.

	Zaslav, president and CEO of Warner Bros. Discovery, shared a video with employees Monday expressing gratitude for their hard work and creativity over the years. (The video, viewed by Variety, is available only on WBD’s internal portal.) Zaslav will exit with the megamerger of Paramount and WBD, scheduled to close Oct. 6, with the new Ellison-run company adopting the name Skydance Corp.
	

	In the video, Zaslav sits alone in a director’s chair in the Loft warehouse at Warner Bros. Studios’ Ranch facility in Burbank, California.

	“For me, it’s been a great honor to be alongside all of you,” Zaslav says, speaking to the camera in the 3-minute video. “I hope you take pride in what you’ve built, what you’ve created, and the role you’ve played in shaping an extraordinary history.” (Read the transcript of his message below.)

	Zaslav’s video includes a montage of Warner Bros. Discovery’s greatest hits, featuring clips from “The Pitt,” “The Lego Movie,” “Barbie,” “One Battle After Another,” “Dune,” “Hacks,” “Friends,” “The House of the Dragon,” “White Lotus,” “Abbott Elementary,” “Sinners,” Discovery’s Shark Week and (of course!) “Harry Potter,” as well as shots from CNN and WBD’s sports programming. According to a company source, Zaslav wanted to share his goodbye message as a video rather than a text memo in order to capture the visuals.
	

	“I can’t wait to see what you do in the years ahead,” Zaslav says. “I’m so grateful for all these years at Warner Bros. Discovery, for the wonderful experiences creating content, telling stories and getting to know so many of you.”

	Zaslav has been among the most highly compensated CEOs in the media biz. In 2025, his pay package totaled $165 million. That included a one-time grant of stock options valued at $109.6 million, which the company awarded to Zaslav on June 12, 2025, for his work on the company’s plan to split into two publicly traded entities (one housing WB’s HBO, HBO Max and studios business; the other largely composed of the linear TV network business along with Discovery+ and other assets). The WBD split into two companies did not proceed because of the deal to sell the company to Paramount Skydance.

	When the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger closes, Zaslav is set to receive a “golden parachute” payout of at least $550 million.

	Over the years, Zaslav and his lieutenants made job cuts across the company as they looked to reduce costs and improve operating efficiency. For full-year 2022, Warner Bros. Discovery had a pro-forma EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization) loss of about $2.1 billion. In 2025, it generated EBITDA profit of $1.4 billion and has been on track for double-digit percentage growth in subscriber-related revenue growth in 2026.

	Here’s a transcript of Zaslav’s farewell message:

	Hello, everyone. I’m here in the scenic Loft on the Warner Bros. lot in Burbank. For the uninitiated, it might look like an empty room. But people here know what spaces like this can become. For decades, worlds have been built here. Sets have gone up, come down and given way to something entirely different.

	If these walls could talk they’d tell stories about extraordinary creativity, craftsmanship and collaboration. They’d tell stories about the people who imagined something that didn’t exist and then found a way to bring it to life. The late nights, the early mornings, the commitment to making something the very best it can be.

	That’s what all of you, all around the world, do every day. You start with an idea, and through talent, expertise and an enormous amount of hard work, turn it into something real. Something that connects with people, stays with them and becomes part of their lives. Over the years, you’ve created countless moments just like that. Stories and characters, games and experiences, that became part of our culture. Journalism that helped people understand the world around them. Moments in sports that brought people to the edge of their seats, and at times, a front-row seat to history itself.
	

	But none of those moments happened on their own. Behind every one of those moments is the work, talent and commitment of everyone who does their part to bring it all to life. And that is what matters. Honoring the work that came before us, doing our part to carry it forward and knowing that the work continues.

	For me, it’s been a great honor to be alongside all of you. I hope you take pride in what you’ve built, what you’ve created and the role you’ve played in shaping an extraordinary history.

	What’s past is prologue. The future waits for each and every one of you. For your spirit, your ingenuity, your creativity and your courage.

	I can’t wait to see what you do in the years ahead. I’m so grateful for all these years at Warner Bros. Discovery, for the wonderful experiences creating content, telling stories and getting to know so many of you. Thank you so much.

schema.headline: David Zaslav Bids Farewell to Warner Bros. Employees in Video on Eve of Skydance Merger Close: ‘It’s Been a Great Honor to Be Alongside All of You’

title: ‘I, Addict’ Creator Javier Giner Unpacks ‘This Solitude,’ a Film ‘About ‘Those Who Keep Functioning While Something Inside Them Is Falling Apart’
description: Basque director Javier Giner‘s “This Solitude” (“Esta Soledad”) recently premiered at the San Sebastián Film Festival’s New Directors section on Sep
body:
Basque director Javier Giner‘s “This Solitude” (“Esta Soledad”) recently premiered at the San Sebastián Film Festival’s New Directors section on Sept. 23. Giner is the creator and co-director of the Disney+ series “I, Addict,” based on his autobiographical book by the same name. It earned lead actor Oriol Pla the International Emmy for Best Actor.

	Also starring Pla, “This Solitude” follows Leo and Lorea after their five-year relationship has ended. Each of them has to figure out how to continue living life on their own in Bilbao. Leo is a struggling actor who has to work as a grocery clerk to make ends meet while taking care of his disabled father. Lorea is a troubled writer who looks to a former prison inmate for companionship. Both must confront their loneliness and unresolved issues and look for meaning in a world that can sometimes feel cruel and scary.
	



	

									Oriol Pla in ‘This Solitude’
	



	“The film is about people who are losing control of their lives. Loneliness may be one of the few truly democratic things in life; what isn’t democratic are the resources we have to survive it,” Giner told Variety.


	The film stars Pal, Marina Salas (“Join Me for Breakfast”), Gemma Martínez, Kai Etxaniz and Itziar Lazkano. Giner co-wrote the film with Luisa Matienzo, who is also one of the film’s producers along with Miguel Torrente. The production companies are Balance Media Entertainment, Fuga de Cuerpos, La Embajada TV and Basajaun Filmak. International sales are being handled by Filmax and they will release the film theatrically in Spain on Oct. 30.



	

									Director Javier Giner, ‘This Solitude’ Photo Credit: David Herranza
	



	Variety interviewed Javier Giner after the film’s premiere in San Sebastián.
	

	There is a loneliness epidemic around the world and this film seems to address it. 

	Javier Giner: I didn’t set out to make a film about the loneliness epidemic. I’m a little wary of starting a film with a theme. This began with the desire to create, more than a film, an emotional state that would stay with the audience after they left the theater.

	I looked around me and saw people with apparently full lives — jobs, friends, partners, phones that never stop, social media — and yet they were profoundly lonely and exhausted. I was fascinated by the contradiction: we’ve never had so many tools to avoid being alone and, paradoxically, so many ways of never truly connecting with anyone.

	Is this story also autobiographical like your book “I, Addict”?

	Giner: Everything I write is autobiographical in some way, but not in the sense that “I, Addict” was, where I was explicitly telling the story of a period in my own life. In “Esta Soledad,” the autobiography is in the gaze and in the emotions: Sadness, family relationships, certain ways of loving, the fear of losing someone, the feeling of not knowing what to do with your life. More and more, what interests me is whether what I write is emotionally true. To me, that is a deeper form of autobiography, and something I find endlessly fascinating.

	The film is also about absent parents, both physically and emotionally. Do you think this is especially true for the new generation?

	Giner: I think every generation inherits from the previous one not only its traumas, but also its emotional vocabulary, including the things it never had words for. The parents in “Esta Soledad” are not monsters. Even when they cause pain, they love their children and they do the best they can. But loving someone and knowing how to love someone are two very different things.

	Children end up living with the emotional consequences of decisions they never made. I think we all spend part of our lives trying to understand what we received from our parents, and another part deciding what we’re going to do with it.

	You chose to work with Oriol Pla again after “I, Addict.”

	Giner: Oriol and I have something more valuable than simply understanding each other: we trust each other completely. And trust allows for things that are far more interesting and profound than comfort.
	

	After “I, Addict,” we had already gone through some very emotionally demanding places together, so now we can arrive on set and barely need to talk. Sometimes a word or a look is enough. Or I can simply tell him, “I don’t know exactly what I’m looking for. Let’s find it together.”

	Oriol can be explosive, physical, unpredictable, almost animalistic, and five seconds later he can do something tiny that breaks your heart. Very few actors can inhabit both of those extremes. As an actor, he’s a Stradivarius, and on top of that he’s an incredible human being. He’s my brother, my partner.

	Bilbao seems to be a central character in the film, sometimes portrayed as lonely, dark and gritty. Would you agree?

	Giner: Yes, although I never wanted to film Bilbao as a sad city, but rather as a state of mind. I wanted to film what almost never gets filmed anymore: not the postcard, but the humidity, the noise, the architecture, the industrial memory, that light that can change completely within a matter of minutes. There is something very physical about the city; at times, it almost seems to weigh on the bodies.

	That connected with Leo and Lorea. Their external world remains exactly where it was while everything inside them has changed completely. The streets are the same, but they no longer mean the same thing. I believe strongly in that: Cities don’t change when we suffer; the way we look at them does. So Bilbao wasn’t there to illustrate their sadness. It had to remain indifferent to it. And paradoxically, that indifference is what ultimately makes the city so deeply emotional.

schema.headline: ‘I, Addict’ Creator Javier Giner Unpacks ‘This Solitude,’ a Film ‘About ‘Those Who Keep Functioning While Something Inside Them Is Falling Apart’

title: Skydance’s High-Wire Act Begins: Wall Street Scrutinizes Strategy for Juggling $80 Billion in Debt  and a Three-Year Runway to Chop it Down
description: David Ellison moved mountains and fought off many detractors in his quest to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery. Now, as the transition is set to formal
body:
David Ellison moved mountains and fought off many detractors in his quest to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery. Now, as the transition is set to formally close on Oct. 6, the high-wire act is about to begin.

	The enlarged entity, to be known as Skydance, will carry a nearly unprecedented level of debt for a large media M&A transaction — a nearly $80 billion chunk — and that leverage will weigh on virtually every decision the company makes over the next three years. By comparison, when Discovery bought WarnerMedia from AT&T, it assumed $43 billion of AT&T’s debt, leaving the new WBD with about $53 billion in gross debt as of June 2022.
	

	Skydance has a tight runway through the end of 2029 to significantly pare down the long-term debt on the company’s books. If Skydance doesn’t hit some very specific targets laid out in its agreements with lenders for reducing its overall leverage ratio, Larry Ellison, the software billionaire and the father of the Skydance CEO, will be on the hook to make up the difference out of his personal wealth.


	Analysts from three major credit ratings agencies — Moody’s Ratings, S&P Global Ratings and Fitch Solutions’ CreditSights — say the company is walking a tightrope of having to manage a difficult post-deal integration process at a time when the entertainment landscape continues to evolve in unpredictable ways. Skydance is counting on several things to go right for its key units — from Paramount Pictures and Warner Bros. to HBO Max and Paramount+ to CNN and CBS — while it also faces competitive pressure to invest big in content and improved technology for the aging infrastructure at the legacy Paramount and Warner Bros. in particular.
	

	RELATED CONTENT: Skydance takes over Warner Bros. Discovery: Everything You Need to Know

	Barring a box office miracle or windfall of streaming subscribers in the coming months, Skydance is projected to operate for all of 2027 with negative cash flow — which will make it harder to be opportunistic in the marketplace. It’s not an impossible feat. But it will require enormous discipline across the organization to focus on priorities and, most importantly, new pipelines for profit.

	“They need to move as quickly as possible to get this leverage down,” says Jawad Hussain, managing director at S&P Global Ratings. “While 2027 is not going to have any cash flow, if [Skydance] does this quickly enough, then by 2028 you’re starting to make money and you can then start paying down your debt. And then in ’29 it can get better. That’s the time frame that they have to do it in.”

	The company has committed to achieving $6 billion operational savings over three years. That process will be hard on the organization as much of it will come from staff cuts to address overlapping operations and redeployment of resources.

	“Until you own the asset, you can’t necessarily fully know what you need to do,” Hussain says. “I would say post-Q3 into the end of the year, and then early next year when they report Q4, we’re hoping to see a nice layout of the strategy and the timelines around that.”

	Robert Fishman, senior analyst for MoffettNathanson Research, also sees Skydance leaders operating in a tough environment of balancing the need to grow the streaming engines — HBO Max and Paramount+ — without starving the linear channels that still generate the majority of the company’s cash flow.

	“The company is going to be forced into choosing where to invest their dollars, led by streaming,” Fishman says. “And they need to make sure that the cash flows they’re shifting toward are not going to be to the detriment of the overall company’s cash flows.”

	The transaction that saw the smaller Paramount Skydance take over the larger WBD was enabled through Byzantine financing structures and a consortium of debt partners that include Middle East sovereign wealth funds.

	The debt piled onto the new company’s balance sheet has sparked intense scrutiny in business and geopolitical circles, although Skydance has consistently assured leaders and Wall Street that the foreign entities will have no governance role or operational influence on the company.
	

	For media biz analysts, the big question in the short term is how David Ellison and his newly recruited co-CEO Ynon Kreiz can make the merger math work. In the view of S&P Global’s Hussain and others, the Skydance deal is putting together two media giants that were already struggling to generate consistent profit and cash flows given all the outside pressures in the marketplace.

	“Paramount itself was generating a little bit of cash flow. Warner Bros. was generating some cash flow — but they both had their issues,” Hussain observes. “So this has been the big issue for a lot of these legacy media companies. We already saw this with Discovery and Warner Bros. merging [in 2022]. We saw this with Viacom and CBS merging [in 2019]. They’ve had a go at it. So the question is: why is this time going to be different?”

	Jason Cuomo, senior VP in the corporate finance group for Moody’s Ratings, believes it will take time before investors can really measure the potential of the company. In that sense, the backstop of Larry Ellison’s extraordinary resources is seen by many as the only way the deal could be completed given how much is at risk. Moody’s has rated Skydance’s debt overall at Ba3, which is one notch below investment grade. That investment rating means the company pays higher interest rates in most cases for the credit facilities and short-term borrowings that are a normal course of business for large enterprises.

	“It’s a massive company that is going through a multiyear restructuring. That’s going to mean a lot of disruption and a lot of change at the highest levels,” says Cuomo.

	“A key support for the credit profile is the controlling shareholder’s [the Ellison family] commitment to backstop the company’s target leverage at the end of 2028 and 2029. If that commitment wasn’t there, our view of this credit profile and the risk would be greater. It effectively will reconcile the divide between what the company hopes to achieve in two to three years and what the commitment is. They’re committed to close that gap. That is one of the material risks that exist.”

	S&P Global and CreditSights give Skydance slightly higher ratings that push them over the edge into investment grade territory that was essential for a company shouldering so much debt. S&P Global and others calculate Skydance in 2026 and 2027 as having a debt-to-earnings ratio of 7. The goal is to chop that down to 3 or less by 2029.
	

	Hunter Martin, senior analyst for telecom, media and cable for CreditSights, says the Street will be watching the company’s financial performance closely. But he echoes Cuomo’s view that it will be impossible to tell after just a few quarters. Martin says he’ll keep a close watch on the near-term fate of the linear channels. As those channels go, so goes the company’s biggest source of cash flow.

	“There’s two big things that are important that we can look at right now: what is happening when it comes to traditional TV networks businesses: CNN, TNT, TBS, the Discovery channels, Nickelodeon, CBS. “They’re in secular decline, but they contribute like 70%-plus of the profits and almost all the free cash flow,” Martin says. “They’ve already been cutting costs, so we want to see how that develops because this is the big profit driver and the big cash generator of the combined business.”

	Martin adds that despite the turmoil around the deal-making process, both Paramount and Warner Bros. come into the deal with operational success stories to tout.

	“Both of these businesses have shown pretty good momentum in recent quarters,” Martin says. “So what we want to see there [is] if they can maintain or improve that momentum after combining.”

	Hussain says he’ll watch how the company handles its tech-stack needs in merging Paramount, HBO Max and Pluto TV FAST channel service. All of the legacy studios have struggled to deliver great digital user experiences a la Netflix. Skydance has a shot to stand tall if it can catch up with Netflix and Disney+ in algorithm and design. Given the Ellison family’s roots in technology (Larry Ellison is co-founder of Oracle), there may be resources available that will turbocharge the inevitable combination of the company’s streaming platforms into a single vertical powered by the same tech engines.

	“The legacy media companies were always at a disadvantage because they didn’t necessarily have the tech backgrounds to figure out the tech part,” Hussain says. “Content is obviously very important. But your ability to distribute and have a good platform is important as well. Netflix has demonstrated that. And you see with YouTube and others how their platforms themselves are also very important in making the customer experience better and all of that stuff. So now you’re bringing in someone who has a far more tech background.”
	

	MoffettNathanson’s Fishman says the company’s content spending priorities in the first year will also be telling. After Skydance bought Paramount in August 2025, its first splashy news announcement was a seven-year commitment to UFC rights at an eye-popping $7.7 billion price tag.

	“One of the biggest things that we’re watching for is the direction of the combined content spending going forward, and where they’re going to look to take some efficiencies,” Fishman says. “And whether sports is going to take an increasing share of that, given upcoming [NFL rights] negotiations, and where streaming fits into [Skydance’s] overall budget as they reallocate resources away from linear.”

	Martin notes that the speed bump Skydance hit in the approval process — the antitrust lawsuit filed by 12 states — cost them probably another $500 million in higher interest fees on short-term debt as rates have inched up.

	“They’re not going to have like any extra cash flow to pay down debt [in 2027] because all these synergies will take some time to realize,” Martin says. “A lot of cost to achieve these synergies that are front-weighted. You have to do redundancies, and you have to pay people [severance fees],” he says. “If you have to do the technological investment to move over to a new platform, you might have to get out of old real estate leases to move everyone to one headquarters. Those are headwinds initially.”

	Martin and other analysts reinforce that Skydance has to juggle a number of spinning plates in real time — against hard deadlines backed by hard numbers.

	“The market knows that basically, they need to deliver on these cost synergies. And they need to grow their profits to reduce debt load and improve their credit metrics,” he says.

title: Mike Leigh’s ‘Tender Loving Care’ to Compete as Comedy at Golden Globes (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Mike Leigh is bringing love and care to the Golden Globes’ comedy race.

	Bleecker Street will submit “Tender Loving Care,” Leigh’s likely final fil
body:
Mike Leigh is bringing love and care to the Golden Globes’ comedy race.

	Bleecker Street will submit “Tender Loving Care,” Leigh’s likely final film, in the musical or comedy categories at the upcoming 84th Golden Globes, Variety has learned exclusively.

	Marion Bailey will compete for best actress in a musical or comedy, where she is expected to face contenders including Julianne Moore (“The Debut”), Inde Navarrette (“Obsession”) and Olivia Wilde (“The Invite”). Kate O’Flynn, Alice Bailey Johnson and Paul Jesson will compete in the supporting acting races, which the Globes do not divide by genre. The submissions mirror the studio’s overall acting strategy heading into the Oscar campaign.
	

	The news comes a week after Focus Features submitted “Obsession,” Curry Barker’s horror breakout, as a comedy — a classification that prompted plenty of head-scratching among awards pundits and moviegoers on social media. Leigh’s film, however, seems like a more natural fit. It can be argued that Leigh has never really made comedies or dramas; rather, he makes films about life, which tends to be both at once.

	“Tender Loving Care” follows Amy (O’Flynn), a London social worker who moves in with her friend and colleague Rosie (Johnson) after a breakup. Meanwhile, Amy’s parents, Birdie (Bailey) and Geoff (Jesson), navigate the indignities of getting older. Drunken singalongs and kitchen dancing sit alongside hospital visits, with the laughs often arriving with a wince attached.

	The last time the Golden Globes classified a Mike Leigh film as a comedy, Sally Hawkins walked away with the best actress prize. That was 18 years ago, for “Happy-Go-Lucky,” with a 21-year-old O’Flynn in a small role that marked her first screen job. Coming off her Emmy win for supporting comedy actress in Apple TV’s “Widow’s Bay,” O’Flynn’s momentum is building. She won the Silver Shell for best leading performance at the San Sebastian Film Festival in September, where the film also took the Golden Shell and the best screenplay prize.
	

	For Bailey, the Globes push represents long-overdue recognition for the veteran performer. Leigh’s real-life partner and a longtime member of his acting company, she previously played Sophia Booth, J.M.W. Turner’s Margate landlady and companion, in his 2014 film “Mr. Turner.” In “Tender Loving Care,” she acts opposite her real-life daughter, Johnson, who plays Amy’s best friend.

	Leigh’s films have earned six Golden Globe nominations across three titles throughout his career, with two of his leading ladies taking home trophies. “Secrets & Lies” scored three nominations, including best motion picture (drama) and supporting actress for Marianne Jean-Baptiste, while Brenda Blethyn won best actress in a drama. Imelda Staunton also earned a nomination in the same category for her critically acclaimed titular role in “Vera Drake.” Then came “Happy-Go-Lucky,” which landed a best motion picture (musical or comedy) nom alongside Hawkins, who won best actress. The film, and Hawkins’ performance, failed to translate into an Oscar nom.

	Shockingly, Leigh himself has never been nominated at the Globes for either directing or screenwriting, despite garnering seven Oscar noms throughout his career. “Topsy-Turvy,” “Another Year,” “Mr. Turner” and “Hard Truths” all came up empty.

	After a 50-year career, Bleecker Street is hoping to get Leigh the recognition he deserves. The company will release “Tender Loving Care” in theaters Dec. 4. The 84th Golden Globe nominations will be announced Monday, Dec. 7, and the ceremony, hosted by Nikki Glaser, is set for Sunday, Jan. 10.

title: Robert Kelker-Kelly, ‘Days of Our Lives’ Actor, Dies at 62
description:
Robert Kelker-Kelly, who played Bo Brady on “Days of Our Lives,” died on Saturday in St. Peters, Missouri. He was 62.

	The St. Peters Police Depart
body:
Robert Kelker-Kelly, who played Bo Brady on “Days of Our Lives,” died on Saturday in St. Peters, Missouri. He was 62.

	The St. Peters Police Department said they responded for a report of an unconscious male who was not breathing. Police noted that he had reportedly complained of chest pain shortly before becoming unresponsive, and the circumstances appeared consistent with a medical event.


	Kelker-Kelly began his acting career playing Sam Fowler on the soap opera “Another World” in 1987. In 1992, he joined “Days of Our Lives,” taking over the role from Peter Reckell. Kelker-Kelly played the character opposite Kristian Alfonso’s Hope Brady and Lisa Rinna‘s Billie Reed before Reckell returned to the role in 1995.
	

	In her memoir, “You Better Believe I’m Gonna Talk About It,” Rinna discussed her difficult working relationship as on-screen love interests with Kelker-Kelly from 1992 to 1995. She said they did not get along in real life, despite filming together “every day, often half naked.”


	Rinna and Kelker-Kelly both joined the daytime show in 1992, and later earned a Soap Opera Digest Award for Hottest Soap Couple in 1995. That same year, they both exited their roles.

	Two years later in 1997, Kelker-Kelly married Miriam Parrish and left Los Angeles, leaving his acting career behind. He earned a certification in airframe and powerplant mechanics. From 2002 to 2003, he was an acting teacher at the Pioneer Valley Performing Arts Charter Public School in South Hadley, Massachusetts, before becoming a professional pilot. He was still teaching and flying up until his death.
	

	He also played Stavros Cassadine on “General Hospital” in 2001, with guest spots in 2002, 2003, 2013 and 2014. Along with his work in television, he acted in several films and TV movies including “Dream for an Insomniac,” “Winter Heat” and “Mr. Write.”

CPR was already in progress while police and EMS were en-route.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Officers and paramedics attempted life-saving measures, but they were unsuccessful.

            Kelker-Kelly made headlines earlier this year after Rinna discussed their contentious relationship in her memoir. She accused him of being verbally abusive, manipulative and playing mind games with her while they worked together on the soap. She also claimed his abrupt departure prompted NBC to provide security for her and Alfonso.
      
    
            Kelker-Kelly did not publicly respond to Rinna's allegations.
